title: Merge sort
objectives: Implement merge sort and derive its running time.
Use the merge step to merge sorted logs and to count inversions.

hints.text: Which two values could be the smallest one left?
Only the two fronts can be the smallest left: everything behind them is larger.
Take the smaller front each time: 2, 3, 4, 5, 9, 10, 12. Then a is empty, so copy what is left of b.

feedback.correct: Eight values out in order, one step each.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the smaller front each time, and empty both lists.

byKey.wbig: You took the larger front. The smaller front must go out first, or the output is out of order.

explain.text: Each step compared two fronts and moved one value out, so eight values took at most seven comparisons. This is a **merge**: linear in the total length.

screens.title: Split until trivial
screens.prose: **Merge sort**: split the list in half, sort each half the same way, then merge the two sorted halves. A list of one value is already sorted.

state.caption: Each call splits its list in half

screens.question: Merging happens once per level above the single values. How many levels of merging does this list of 8 need?

hints.text: How many times can you halve 8 before you reach 1?
These are the single values at the bottom.
8 splits to 4, then 2, then 1: three halvings. So there are 3 levels of merging back up.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the halvings from 8 down to 1.

byKey.eight: You counted the values. The levels count halvings, and 8 halves to 1 in three steps.
byKey.seven: You counted the merges, seven in all. They sit on three levels.
byKey.four: You counted the rows of the tree, including the single values, which need no merging.

explain.text: The tree has $\log_2 8 = 3$ levels of splitting. On the way back up, each level merges all 8 values in some groups. So each level costs about 8 steps.

screens.title: Write the merge
screens.prose: Return a new sorted list with every value of `a` and `b`. Take from `a` when the fronts are equal. Leave the inputs unchanged.
screens.question: Write `merge(a, b)` for two sorted lists.

widget.how: Check runs 9 hidden tests. They include the example, empty lists, duplicates, a tail left in either list, unchanged inputs, and two lists of 50,000.

hints.text: Keep an index into each list and compare the two fronts.
When one list runs out, values are left in the other.
While both have values, append the smaller front (`a` on a tie) and move its index. Then `extend` with `a[i:]` and `b[j:]`.

feedback.correct: Every value comes out once, in order, in one pass.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-6: Test 6 leaves 5 in `a` after `b` runs out. You kept the tail of `b` but dropped the tail of `a`; extend with both `a[i:]` and `b[j:]`.
byKey.test-2: Test 2 has an empty `a`. The loop never runs, so everything comes from the tail of `b`.
byKey.test-9: Test 9 merges 100,000 values. A recursive merge hits Python's recursion limit there, and `out = out + [x]` is too slow. Walk two indices in one loop.

explain.text: Each comparison moves one value out, so a merge of $n$ values makes at most $n - 1$ comparisons. The tail is already sorted and larger than everything taken, so it goes on the end as it is.

screens.title: Write merge sort
screens.prose: `merge` from before is in the starter. Now split, sort each half by calling `merge_sort` itself, and merge. Return a new list.

state.caption: Each call splits its list in half

screens.question: Write `merge_sort(xs)`.

widget.how: Check runs 8 hidden tests. They include the example, empty and one-value lists, two values, duplicates, 20,000 values in reverse order, and an unchanged input.

hints.text: What list needs no sorting at all? That is the base case.
Each call splits its list at `len(xs) // 2`.
If `len(xs) <= 1`, return `list(xs)`. Else `mid = len(xs) // 2` and return `merge(merge_sort(xs[:mid]), merge_sort(xs[mid:]))`.

feedback.correct: It sorts 20,000 reversed values quickly, where insertion sort would need 200 million comparisons.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. If it was `RecursionError`, your base case misses lists of one value.
byKey.test-7: Test 7 sorts 20,000 values. Splitting off one value at a time nests 20,000 calls, past the recursion limit: split at the middle.

explain.text: The base case `len(xs) <= 1` covers both the empty list and a single value. Every other call splits into two strictly smaller halves, so the recursion always ends.

screens.title: Equal prices
screens.prose: We merge sort three trades by price. The merge takes from the left half when prices are equal, `a[i] <= b[j]`. The split is `[A]` and `[B, C]`.
screens.question: In what order do they come out?

options.why: You let C pass A on the tie. With `<=` the merge takes A, from the left half, first.
You sorted from high to low. Merge sort here puts the lowest price first.
You kept arrival order. B is cheaper, so it comes out before A.

hints.text: Sort `[B, C]` first. Then merge `[A]` with it.
A and C tie at £101. The tie goes to the left half.
`[B, C]` stays B, C. Merge `[A]` with `[B, C]`: B is cheaper, so B. Then A and C tie, and `<=` takes A. Then C.

feedback.correct: B, then A before C: equal prices keep arrival order.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which half wins a tie?

explain.text: A sits in the left half because it arrived first. Taking from the left on a tie keeps it ahead of C. So merge sort is **stable**; with `<` instead of `<=` it would not be.

options.text: Python's recursion limit is set too low

You rounded the split up. Then `mid` is 1 and `xs[:mid]` is the whole list, the same loop on the other side.

hints.text: Work out `mid`, `xs[:mid]` and `xs[mid:]` for `xs = [7]`.
The traceback says the calls went on and on.
`mid = 1 // 2 = 0`, so `xs[:0]` is `[]` and `xs[0:]` is `[7]`. The call on `[7]` repeats for ever.

feedback.correct: A one-value list splits into nothing and itself, so the call repeats.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Split `[7]` by hand.

byKey.merge: You blamed `merge`. It never runs; the call on `[7]` calls itself on `[7]` again first.
byKey.limit: You blamed the limit. The list never gets shorter, so no limit is enough.
byKey.round: You rounded the split up. That puts the whole list in the left half instead: the same problem.

explain.text: A split must make both halves strictly shorter. That fails for one value, whichever way we round. So one value must be a base case: `if len(xs) <= 1`.

screens.title: Why $n \log n$
screens.prose:
Let $T(n)$ be the steps merge sort takes on $n$ values. Two half-size sorts and a merge give
$$T(n) = 2\,T(n/2) + n.$$
We sum the work level by level of the tree.

state.caption: Each call splits its list in half

screens.question: Put the steps in order.

lines.text: Level 0: one call merges all $n$ values, cost $n$ (the $+\,n$ term)
Level $k$: $2^k$ calls each merge $n/2^k$ values, cost $2^k \cdot n/2^k = n$
Sizes halve until they reach 1, so there are $\log_2 n$ levels that merge
Total: $n$ per level times $\log_2 n$ levels is $n \log_2 n$

hints.text: Start at the top of the tree with the cost of one merge.
This level has two calls of half size.
Top level costs $n$. Every level costs $n$, because more calls each merge less. There are $\log_2 n$ levels. Multiply.

feedback.correct: Every level costs $n$, and there are $\log_2 n$ levels.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find one level's cost before counting the levels.

explain.text: For 8 values: 3 levels of about 8 steps each, so about 24, against 28 for insertion sort's worst case. For a million: 20 levels of a million, against half a trillion. The merge needs a new list, so merge sort uses $O(n)$ extra memory.

screens.title: How out of order
screens.prose: Two analysts rank six stocks. List analyst B's ranks in analyst A's order. A pair of stocks the two rank in opposite order is an **inversion**. Counting them measures disagreement, as Kendall's rank correlation does.

state.caption: B's ranks, in A's order: 3 inversions out of 15 pairs

screens.question: Write `count_inversions(xs)`: the number of pairs `i < j` with `xs[i] > xs[j]`, in $O(n \log n)$.

widget.how: Check runs 10 hidden tests: the ranking, empty and one-value lists, sorted and reversed lists, and equal values (not inversions). One has 20,000 values, where checking every pair is too slow, and one checks the input is unchanged.

hints.text: Merge sort each half, counting inside each. What does the merge add?
Once this 1 is taken from the right half, it jumps every left value still waiting.
In the merge, each time you take from the right half, add `len(left) - i`. The left values still waiting are all bigger. Return the count from the halves plus the merge.

feedback.correct: The same split and merge as the sort, with a counter, so $O(n \log n)$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-8: Test 8 has equal values, which are not inversions. Take from the left on a tie, `<=`, so equal pairs are not counted.
byKey.test-9: Test 9 has 20,000 values, about 200 million pairs. Checking every pair is too slow; count during the merge.

explain.text: Here 3 of 15 pairs disagree, so Kendall's tau is $1 - 2 \times 3/15 = 0.6$. A value taken from the right half jumps over every left value still waiting. Each jump is one inversion, counted in bulk.

screens.title: Two venues
screens.prose: Each venue's log of `(time, venue, size)` is sorted by time. Merge them into one log by time. On a tie, put the first log's trade first.

state.caption: Each column is sorted by time

screens.question: Write `merge_logs(a, b)`.

widget.how: Check runs 6 hidden tests: the two logs, the same logs swapped, and an empty log on either side. The others have two empty logs and a single trade in each.

hints.text: This is `merge`, comparing only the times.
These two trades share a time. The first log's trade goes first.
Compare `a[i][0] <= b[j][0]`: take from `a` on a tie. Add both tails at the end.

feedback.correct: One pass over both logs, ties to the first log.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-2: Test 2 swaps the logs, so at 09:00:03 the CXE trade, now in the first log, comes first.
byKey.test-3: Test 3 has an empty first log, so the answer is the second log as it stands.

explain.text: Comparing whole tuples would break ties by venue name, not by log. Comparing times with `<=` keeps the merge stable. Each trade is handled once, so the cost is linear in the total.

screens.title: Too big for memory
screens.prose: A year of ticks is 200 GB, and the machine has 16 GB of memory. You need the file sorted by time.

state.caption: Sorted runs of about 15 GB each, written to disk

screens.question: Which plan works?

options.text: Sort memory-sized chunks, write each sorted run to disk, then merge the runs from their fronts

options.why: You loaded 200 GB into 16 GB of memory. It does not fit.

options.text: Insertion sort the file on disk, one tick at a time
options.why: You chose an $O(n^2)$ sort with a disk access per step. It would take years.

options.text: Sort each chunk and join the sorted chunks end to end
options.why: You joined the runs without merging. Each run is sorted, but the joined file is not.

hints.text: A merge only ever looks at the front of each list.
Each run is sorted on its own.
Sort 13 chunks of about 15 GB in memory, one at a time. Then merge the 13 runs, keeping only each run's front in memory.

feedback.correct: This is **external sorting**: sort in memory, merge on disk.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which plan never needs more than the memory you have?

explain.text: A merge reads each run from its front and writes the output in order. So memory holds only a buffer per run, not the whole file. Databases sort large tables this way.

ideas: Merging two sorted lists takes the smaller front each time, then copies the leftover tail: linear time.
Merge sort splits in half until one value is left, then merges back up: $\log_2 n$ levels of $n$ work each.
It is stable and $O(n \log n)$ on every input, but needs $O(n)$ extra memory.

formula.name: Merge sort's recurrence
formula.note: Each of the $\log_2 n$ levels costs $n$.

summary.trap: A base case that stops only at the empty list recurses for ever on one value. A merge that forgets the tail drops values.

quiz.question: What does `merge([1, 4, 9], [2, 3])` return?

options.why: You assumed the tail is added. This version returns as soon as `b` is empty, dropping 4 and 9.
The loop stops when `b` runs out, before 4 is compared with anything.
The loop condition keeps both indices in range, so nothing fails loudly.

feedback.correct: It silently drops the tail, 4 and 9.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. When does the loop stop, and what is left?

explain.text: After 1, 2 and 3, `b` is empty and the loop ends. Nothing copies `a[i:]`, so 4 and 9 are lost. Always extend with both tails.

quiz.prose: We merge a sorted list of 40 values with a sorted list of 25 values.
quiz.question: At most how many comparisons does the merge make?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each comparison moves one value out.

byKey.total: You counted every value. The last value goes out with no comparison, because the other list is empty.
byKey.product: You compared every pair. A merge only ever compares the two fronts.

explain.text: Each comparison sends one value out. At worst one list empties only when one value is left, so $40 + 25 - 1 = 64$.

quiz.prose: Merge sort takes 1 second on a million prices.
quiz.question: About how long on two million?

options.why: You used $O(n^2)$. Merge sort is $O(n \log n)$.
Twice the values need at least twice the merging.
You multiplied by $\log_2 n$ again. Only one extra level is added.

feedback.correct: Twice the values and one more level: about 2.1 seconds.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare $2n\log_2(2n)$ with $n \log_2 n$.

explain.text: The ratio is $\dfrac{2n \log_2 (2n)}{n \log_2 n} = 2 \times \dfrac{21}{20} = 2.1$ for $n = 10^6$. Doubling $n$ adds one level of merging.

quiz.prose: You compare merge sort with insertion sort on a long list.
quiz.question: Which statement is right?

options.text: Merge sort is faster but needs $O(n)$ extra memory for merging
Merge sort is faster and sorts in place
options.why: You assumed it works in place. The merge writes into a new list.
With `<=` the merge takes the left value on a tie, so equal values keep their order.

options.text: Both are $O(n^2)$ in the worst case
options.why: Merge sort always does $\log_2 n$ levels of $n$ work: $O(n \log n)$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Where does the merge put its output?

explain.text: Each merge builds a new list as long as its inputs, so merge sort needs $O(n)$ extra memory. In exchange it is $O(n \log n)$ on every input and stable.
